zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The scan, not the index, determines the diplomatic text, typography, and physical lineation.

runs.text: tecidos como Tçuzzura que tem a ſella de

lines.note: This continues the saddle-lining definition from the preceding page: woven material like tsuzura is placed underneath the saddle. Read the damaged word as ſella, not the OCR fll; Tçuzzura is a Japanese term embedded in the italic Portuguese. There is no hyphen after de.
This short continuation completes de baixo, describing the underside of the saddle. Retain the physical break between de and baixo and the final full stop.

runs.text: Papel, ou eſcrito como ſinal de man-

lines.note: Kitte denotes a paper or written authorization to have something handed over. The enlarged initial belongs to Qitte, not gite; restore Papel and eſcrito from the visible type. The final man- continues mandar on the next row.
The authorization orders delivery of some object. Keep the nasal abbreviation in algũa and the printed &c.; dar completes the divided mandar, rather than starting an independent phrase.
Kitto is labelled an adverb and glossed as hurriedly. The space around the enlarged initial is typographic, not a word boundary; retain Apreßadamente with the printed ß form.
This kiwa entry means the edge or limit of something. Restore capital Q; the Portuguese keeps the contraction dalgũa and its abbreviated nasal vowel.
A separate kiwa entry concerns a moment or occasion. Its example starts sono kiwa-ni; retain the visible hyphen after qiua, which divides the phrase across physical rows.

runs.text: Vindo a eße termo, ou inſtante.

lines.note: The example means coming to that point or moment. Keep roman ni natte and the italic explanation, including eße and the original Portuguese spelling and punctuation.
Kyūaku is explained by furuki aku, an old evil or longstanding bad habit. Preserve the space before acu and the caron on ǔ; the gloss has historical antigua, not modern antiga.
The example means reforming old wrongdoing. Read Qiǔ rather than Quǔ and preserve acuuo as printed; Enmendar is the historical Portuguese form and continues into the next line.
The objects of reform are bad customs and old habits. The damaged first letter of habitos is h, not b; no accent is supplied to maos or habitos beyond what is visible.

runs.text: Caſca de hũa certa aruore que ſerue

lines.note: Kiwada is identified here as bark from a certain tree. Preserve Qiuada and hũa; the description of the bark’s uses continues below rather than forming a second entry.
The bark is used for dyeing and medicine. Keep pera in both positions and the historical noun mezinha; the line finishes the Qiuada entry.

Kiwamari is the intransitive verb for becoming settled or reaching a limit. The Portuguese ends in a nasal abbreviation, aßẽ-, which combines with tarſe below; retain both the tilde and the line-final hyphen.
The gloss continues with being settled or entirely completed. The paragraph sign introduces waga shindai; retain roman Va- as the first physical fragment of that example.
Waga shindai koko ni kiwamaru describes one’s condition or fortunes reaching their limit here. The row joins Va- above to ga and begins the italic Portuguese translation with Meu eſtado.
The first example’s translation ends with reaching its conclusion or resting here. A new example, saigo kiwamaru, begins after the paragraph sign; qi- must remain on this row.
Read uamaru, completing qiuamaru across the break. The damaged gloss is Eſtar na derradeira ſem eſperan-, describing being at the last extremity without hope; retain the final hyphen.
This completes eſperanças de viuer, hope of living. The initial ç belongs to the divided Portuguese word; the short line is not an independent entry or stray text.

The noun kiwame means completion, end, or conclusion. Restore m in Qiuame and Conſumaçaõ, and read fim rather than fin. Preserve the historical nasal ending and the tightly printed ouremate rather than regularizing its spacing.
This is the corresponding transitive verb, to complete or bring something to its limit. The headword is followed by a comma before uru, not the OCR full stop; keep algũa abbreviated.

Eiga o kiwamuru means enjoying prosperity to the utmost. Retain the tightly joined Gozarde from the aligned text on reinspection, rather than introducing a word space; keep the roman example distinct from its italic translation.
The translation names prosperity and riches; prosperidades has no securely printed nasal tilde here. The next example begins with kōmyō, a distinguished name or reputation, retaining both carons.
The expression kōmyō o kiwamuru is translated as gaining a great name. Read Alcançar rather than Alçançar; retain the abbreviated cõ at the end and its continuation on the next row.

The reputation is won through deeds in war. The apparent accents in the OCR proezas and guerra are interference rather than secure accents; the next example, ri o kiwamuru, begins in roman type and ends with a printed hyphen.

runs.text: Dar as milhores razoẽs que ſe podẽ dar.

lines.note: The gloss describes giving the best possible reasons. Restore the word divisions in Dar as milhores razoẽs; preserve milhores, the tilde on e in razoẽs, and the nasal abbreviation podẽ.

The quotation means exhausting the truth and fully developing the reasoning before speaking. The u in Macotouo is poorly inked and can resemble i; Macotouo is the chosen reading from the remaining strokes and the particle construction, with some uncertainty. The final no- continues notamaiqereba below; qiuamete is roman throughout, without an added accent.

This finishes notamaiqereba and gives the source abbreviation Taif., followed by book 20. Retain the roman Japanese and citation label, with the bibliographical Lib. 20. in italic; the last numeral is not part of the example sentence.

runs.text: Dizendo toda a verdade, & arrezoando ma-

lines.note: The Portuguese paraphrase says speaking the whole truth and reasoning admirably. Restore Dizendo, toda, and arrezoando from the type; ma- is the first fragment of marauilhoſamente on the next row.
This short row completes marauilhoſamente, admirably or wonderfully. Keep the historical u spelling and long s rather than modernizing the adverb.
Kyūba is explained as bushi no michi, the warrior’s way. The badly corrupted OCR is recoverable as Qiǔba, Buxino michi, and Exercicio, ou arte; the military qualification follows below.

The definition completes military practice or art, then gives kyūba ni tazusawaru, to engage in the warrior’s calling. Keep the roman example after the paragraph sign and the incomplete Portuguese Ser at the end.

runs.text: ſoldado, ou profeßar a arte militar. ¶

lines.note: The first example is translated as being a soldier or professing the military art. The type has profeßar and militar, not the OCR profeſar and mililar; a second example begins with the divided Qiǔ-.
Kyūba no ie ni umaruru means being born into a warrior’s household. Preserve the historical Nacer and roman vmaruru, whose initial v represents the vowel in this spelling system.

runs.text: ſoldado, ou deſcender de caſta de ſoldados.

lines.note: The translation continues with descent from a lineage of soldiers. Read deſcender and caſta, not the heavily corrupted OCR words; the full stop ends the Qiǔba entry.
Kyūbin is an urgent messenger or communication, explained by isogi no tayori. Restore the caron and internal letters in Qiǔbin, and the long s in Menſageiro; its second gloss continues below.
The second gloss is a hurried bearer or courier. Join the OCR porta dor as the single printed word portador and retain the ß in apreßado.
Kyūbyō is a sudden or rapidly developing illness. Restore the two carons and the syllable bi in the headword; the Portuguese reads Doença repentina, ou acelerada, with co- continuing como below.
The definition gives severe fevers as an example of an acute illness. Initial mo completes como from the preceding line, and the printed &c. closes the entry.
Kyūbun denotes a stipend or wage. Restore Qiǔbun and Eſtipendio, retaining the unaccented historical form; the example begins after the paragraph sign and divides Qiǔ-bunuo across rows.

The alternatives mean receiving or giving this wage. Read toru, not torua, and daſu. The provisional font boundary after upright Toma is retained, with the corrected r in the italic run; do not regularize the mixed typography merely because Tomar is a Portuguese word.
The short line completes the phrase about receiving or paying the wage. Jornal is the historical noun for daily pay here, not a newspaper; preserve its final full stop.

This kyūka entry means summer. It is an independent headword at the left margin, not an indented continuation. The following provisional ID c1-l044 duplicated this same physical row; the line is retained here once, with its caron and nasal vowel.
A separate kyūka entry is explained as furui eda, an old branch. Restore the headword, Furui, and Ramo velho from the damaged text; this is not a second copy of the summer sense.
The example says an old branch does not produce flowers. The final verb reads xǒjezu, not xǒjecu; retain the caron and the negative Portuguese não, which continues below.
This completes the statement that the old branch does not flower. The final S. is a printed register marker, not an additional headword; restore florece rather than the OCR fteree.

Kyūchi is glossed by chijin and Portuguese Amigo. The damaged synonym reads Chijn, with the descender of j visible; preserve this spelling rather than inserting another vowel. The discarded provisional c1-l048 represents overlapping OCR noise from this row, not a separate physical line.

Kyūchō is a bird brought to extremity, explained by kiwamatta tori. Restore Qiǔchô, preserving the different marks on ǔ and ô. The Portuguese has Paßaro and vè with a grave accent; the tightly joined queſe is retained from the aligned text rather than regularized.

runs.text: em ſummo aperto como acoçado do falcão, &c.

lines.note: The bird is in extreme distress, for example pursued by a falcon. Preserve ſummo, the cedilla in acoçado, and the nasal spelling falcão; the row ends the initial definition.
The proverb begins with a distressed bird entering someone’s bosom. Restore the printed paragraph sign and the full headword; toqinba and the divided cari- are retained as historical spellings.
The hunter too saves the bird: caribito-mo continues across the row boundary. Keep taſuqu as printed rather than supplying a modern ending, and preserve the Portuguese hyphen in acoça-.

runs.text: do ſe mete no ſeyo atè o caçador o ſalua. Pro-

lines.note: The translation says that even a hunter saves a pursued bird which takes refuge in the bosom. Retain ſeyo, atè, and ſalua; Pro- begins the abbreviated proverb label continued below.

runs.text: uerb. que ſe acomoda aos perſeguidos, aos quaes

lines.note: The usage explanation applies the proverb to persecuted people. Initial uerb. completes Prouerb.; retain the historical relative pronoun quaes and its continuation.

runs.text: os meſmos perſeguidores perdoão vẽdoos em

lines.note: Even the persecutors forgive when they see their victims in misery. Preserve perdoão and the abbreviated nasal form vẽdoos, without inserting a hyphen or expanding the missing nasal letter.
This short row completes the description of extreme misery. The tilde belongs to u in ſũma; retain the unaccented miſeria and the final full stop.
Kyūchū means inside the imperial palace, explained by Dairi no uchi. The final headword vowel is ǔ, not the OCR ô, and vchi begins with v; the Portuguese continues on the next row.
Reaes completes paços reaes, royal or imperial palaces. Retain the historical vowel sequence and the short continuation as a separate physical line.
Kyūkō is an old friendship or connection, explained by furuki yoshimi. Retain the carons and the nasal abbreviation cõ-, which continues as converſação across the break.
The continuation completes the old friendship or acquaintance gloss. Keep uerſação as the second part of the broken word and antigua as printed, rather than modernizing to antiga.

This distinct kyūkō entry concerns longstanding services, not friendship. The scan has ô here, unlike the preceding cǒ entry; restore Seruiços antiguos and the example Qiǔcôno, preserving the paragraph sign.

runs.text: Homem que tem feito muitos ſeruiços,

lines.note: Kyūkō no hito is a person who has rendered many services. Keep the Japanese continuation fito in roman and the Portuguese comma, which links the description to the next row.
The person’s services are also of long standing. Retain the ampersand and the short italic continuation rather than merging it into the previous physical line.
Kyūkon is an old grudge, explained by furuki urami. Read antiguas, not the OCR antizuas; the initial v in vrami is part of the historical romanization.
The example describes dispelling accumulated grievances. Restore the entire roman Qiǔconuo after Vt, rather than leaving its Q inside an italic OCR fragment; retain ſanzuru as printed.

runs.text: as queixas vingandoſe, ou ſatisfazendoſe. S.

lines.note: The gloss explains release of grievances through vengeance or obtaining satisfaction. Remove the OCR’s extra r from ſatisfazendoſe and preserve the final printed S. marker.
A second kyūkon entry means extreme exhaustion, explained by kiwamatta kutabire. The caron is damaged but traceable; preserve the separate entry and the incomplete Portuguese comparison.
The phrase completes great or extreme weariness. Retain the double m in ſummo and the long s and cedilla in canſaço.

runs.text: Qiǔcut. i, Qino tçumaru coto, l, taicut.

lines.note: Kyūkutsu is explained by ki no tsumaru koto, with taikutsu as an alternative. The synonym begins with Qino, not Cino; retain the historical final t in both Qiǔcut and taicut and the roman i, and l, markers.
The Portuguese gloss describes weariness or oppression of the heart. Preserve Enfadamento and abafamento as printed, without recasting this historical sense as a modern diagnosis.
The example means relieving the heart or easing its constraint. Preserve noburu and the paragraph sign; the Portuguese word coração is divided after cora-.
The continuation completes coração and adds recreating or refreshing oneself. Keep the initial cedilla and the reflexive spelling recrearſe, with the entry’s closing full stop.

runs.text: Exame que ſe faz das letras dalguem

lines.note: Kyūdai is described through an examination of someone’s learning. Restore letras from letas; dalguem is retained as the printed contraction, without a supplied accent.

runs.text: pera o aleuantar a algum grao, ou dignidade.

lines.note: The examination serves to raise the person to a rank or dignity. Read dignidade, not the OCR digniãade, and preserve pera, aleuantar, and grao as historical spellings.
The short example forms a verb with suru. Keep Vt, italic and the Japanese expression roman, including the long s used in ſuru and the headword’s caron.
Kyūden is explained by miya and ie and glossed as palaces of kings or princes. Preserve the separate Japanese words and capital Reis; the gloss continues on the next line.
This completes the palaces-of-kings-or-princes definition. The printed principes is unaccented, and its full stop closes the entry.

runs.text: Adorar, ou venerar noue vezes co-

lines.note: Kyūhai refers here to making nine acts of reverence. The headword uses the historical f spelling, Qiǔfai, not the OCR h; restore Adorar and venerar and retain co- at the line end.
The act is described as customary among the Chinese. Initial mo completes como, and Chinas is the printed historical ethnonym; do not replace it with a modern term.
Kyūfu means decay or corruption, explained by kuchi and kusari. Preserve the comma between the Japanese glosses and the line-final cor-, which continues corromperſe.
The short line completes corromperſe, to become corrupted or rotten. It belongs to the preceding definition and retains the reflexive suffix without an inserted hyphen.
Kyūgaku is explained as furuki manabi, old or established learning. Restore Qiǔgacu, manabi, and Estudo rather than Estado; conſuma- carries its printed division into the next row.

runs.text: do, ou antiguo, & de muitos annos.

lines.note: The learning is described as mature, old, and of many years. Retain antiguo and the double n in annos; do completes conſumado across the physical break.
Kyūji is identified with yaitō or yaibi, moxibustion. Preserve Yaitô and the historical f in yaifi; the Portuguese literally describes applications of fire and prints Botoẽs with a tilde on e.
The example means applying moxa, literally giving the fire applications described above. Restore the omitted paragraph sign and retain the nasal spelling botoẽs in the italic Portuguese.
Kyūjo refers to women serving in the imperial palace. Restore Qiǔgio and Dairino tçucai vonna from the damaged OCR; the Portuguese is printed Molhe-, with o, and continues on the next row.

runs.text: res que ſeruem dentro do Dairi.

lines.note: This completes Molheres and explains service inside the Dairi. Dairi is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese sentence and remains italic here pending any human whole-word font adjustment.
Kyūjū is equated with kyūmon, the nine gates of the palace. Preserve the carons, the historical gi spelling, and the roman synonym after i,; the Portuguese continues below.

runs.text: os paços do Dairi por todas as partes ao redor.

lines.note: The gates are described as distributed around the Dairi. Read Dairi without the OCR’s extra accented a; the Japanese palace term occurs within the Portuguese explanation and the row closes the entry.
Kyūgo is explained by sukui and mamoru, saving and protecting. Restore ſaluar with its visible a; guar- retains the printed division of guardar across rows.
The continuation completes guardar and ends with the printed S. usage marker. This very short row is part of the definition, not furniture.
This separate kyūgo entry concerns an ending, explained by yamu toki. Read capital Yamu and Termo, ou fim; preserve the paragraph sign and the final divided Qiǔ-.
The example states that there will be no end. Read Não rather than the OCR paragraph-sign fragment, and retain auera without supplying a modern accent.
Kyūgoku is completion or the ultimate limit, linked to kiwamari. Restore the full headword and retain the verbal continuation ru and final S. marker; the gloss ends here.
Kyūgyū is explained literally as nine cattle, kokonotsu no ushi. Restore Qiǔguiǔ and the carons; the Portuguese full stop precedes separate bottom furniture, which is not part of this body row.
